docs.title: phantom — Development Plan & Roadmap
docs.text: Status: v0.1, for review · Owner: Captain · Date: 2026-10-24 Scope: the physics of a gate-defined spin-qubit device as a library: from gate layout and material stack to charge, readout and spin, with disorder and fabrication defects drawn from a catalog. Consumers: qdt (as a simulated backend), agent evaluation, hosted training scenarios, device-physics studies.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: Real tune-up is hard because of what is not known about a device: its disorder, its defects, its valley splittings. No model predicts a particular device's tune-up at runtime, and this one does not try. phantom produces device instances that behave like real devices of their class — the right kinds of faults at the right rates, the right sweep-rate dependence, the right readout behaviour — and runs them cheaply enough to be swept ten thousand times by a tuning loop. Its claims are statistical (ADR 0002).

docs.title: 2. Two tiers (ADR 0001)
docs.text:
• Compile once. Expensive physics runs once per device instance: electrostatics for a layout and stack, screening, disorder placement, valley-splitting draws. Output: a compiled device — parameter fields and functions the runtime consumes (lever-arm fields, Hubbard parameters as functions of gate voltage, tunnel rates, sensor coupling, noise spectra).
  • Run cheap. The runtime layers evaluate a compiled device at a gate point in well under a millisecond: charge ground state, rates, sensor signal, noise samples, spin dynamics for a few qubits. A tune-up never waits on a solver; a scenario is compiled before it is served.

docs.title: 3. Layers (ADR 0004) — each imports only downward
docs.text:
Layer Owns Runtime-capable form Offline form layout Gate polygons, stack (2DEG depth, dielectrics), material class (SiGe, MOS) — — electrostatics V(r; gate vector) and its basis per gate Closed-form polygonal-gate potentials over a 2DEG (Davies–Larkin–Stern) FEM Poisson, Thomas–Fermi screening, via a wrapped external solver disorder Static potential perturbations and their generators, from the catalog Precomputed perturbation fields Placement draws valley Valley splitting per dot (Si) A draw from a distribution for the material and dot size — (atomistic is out of scope) charge Dots, barriers, few-electron Hubbard/CI, parameter functions t(V), U, V_ij Diagonalize small matrices per gate point — readout Lead tunnel rates, rate equations, latching, charge sensor (SET) response, RF reflectometry, noise processes (fluctuators, 1/f, telegraph, drift) All cheap — spin Zeeman with gate-dependent g, exchange J(ε, t_c), spin–orbit/EDSR, hyperfine, T₁, T₂*, Pauli spin blockade Lindblad for ≤3 qubits; Monte Carlo over noise — optimum For a compiled device: the best achievable operating point, lattice, sensor sensitivity, and (with spin) readout fidelity and coherence Cheap — compile Turns layout + material + a catalog draw + seed into a compiled device — Minutes per instance

qdt-sim's DoubleDotModel and noise models are the seed of charge and readout (Step 1 migrates them).

docs.title: 4. What a consumer gets (ADR 0003)
docs.text:
• compile(layout, material, draw, seed) -> Device — a compiled, serialisable device instance with a model_version.
  • Device.at(gate_vector) -> State (charge configuration, rates, sensor signal); Device.measure(...) for readout and spin outcomes; noise advanced by explicit time steps.
  • Device.truth — the hidden parameters, and optimum(Device) — the best achievable results. Consumers that must hide truth from a user (a tuning loop, a product) simply do not hand it over.
  • Reproducibility: parameters + seed + version → identical output.
  • No instruments, no measurement vocabulary, no users: the adapter that turns a Device into a qdt stand lives in qdt and pins a phantom release.

docs.title: 5. The defect and material catalog (ADR 0006)
docs.text: docs/catalog/ is data a human fills in: each entry names a defect or material trait, the layer it perturbs, the parameter and its distribution, a severity knob, the signature it leaves in a tune-up, and a source. disorder and compile read it. The catalog is the part only an experienced tuner can write; its entries are filed as issues for that reason.

docs.title: 6. Validation: test ladder, reference library, gallery (ADR 0007, 0008, 0009; 0005 superseded)
docs.text:

docs.text:
Step Name Exit in one line Detail 0 Bootstrap Repo, CI, layer skeletons, catalog template, first ADRs steps/00-bootstrap.md 1 Charge and readout core qdt-sim's model and noise migrated; parameter functions; reproducibility contract proven steps/01-charge-readout-core.md 2 Layout and closed-form electrostatics A layout + stack gives V(r) and lever-arm fields in microseconds; two-dot lattice emerges from a layout steps/02-layout-electrostatics.md 3 Disorder and the fault models Catalog draws perturb the potential; unintentional dots, leaky barriers, switchers, drift appear for physical reasons steps/03-disorder-faults.md 4 Readout physics Lead rates, latching, sweep-rate dependence, sensor and RF response, 1/f and telegraph noise from fluctuator ensembles steps/04-readout.md 5 Valley Statistical valley splitting per dot; PSB consequences steps/05-valley.md 6 Spin Few-qubit dynamics under pulses; readout fidelity, T₁, T₂* steps/06-spin.md 7 Compile and optimum Offline FEM electrostatics wrapped; compile(); optimum() for every layer steps/07-compile-optimum.md 8 qdt cutover qdt-sim becomes an adapter pinning phantom; qdt's golden files regenerated once steps/08-qdt-cutover.md

Steps 1–4 give faithful faults and are the body of the work; 5–6 extend to spin; 7 closes the loop; 8 is coordinated with qdt. 1 and 2 can start together.

docs.title: 8. Open decisions
docs.text: # Decision State 1 Which external electrostatics solver to wrap at Step 7 Open; closed-form first 2 Hubbard vs. full CI as the default charge solver Open; Hubbard first, CI where PSB needs orbitals 3 Serialisation of a compiled device (format, size) Open; must be versioned and diffable 4 Catalog file format and schema (YAML proposed) Open; ADR 0006 proposes 5 Whether holes (Ge) join the material classes Open; electrons in Si first

docs.title: 9. Success criteria
docs.text:
1. A tune-up loop runs against a phantom at ≥ 10⁴ gate points per second per core.
  2. The fault catalog's entries each produce their signature in a stability diagram, with a P0 or P1 test.
  3. Reproducibility holds across platforms in CI.
  4. qdt's adapter is under 300 lines and contains no physics.
  5. A P1 suite of at least five published results reproduces within stated tolerance.

docs.title: How the models fit together (ADR 0011)
docs.text: Two diagrams and a runtime ledger, kept current with every change to a model. The first diagram is drawn by hand and says how a measurement is produced from a gate vector: which model feeds which, in the order the physics happens. Whoever adds or rewires a model updates it in the same pull request. The second is generated from the imports in src/phantom by scripts/model_graph.py and checked in CI, so it can never be stale. The ledger records what each model and each protocol costs to run: declared budgets from the protocol files, and the last measurement recorded by scripts/gallery.py --record.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• A shorted plunger–middle-barrier pair merges the two dots into one at the clean operating point; the two-dot CI model cannot represent it, so the fault protocol shows the plunger–outer-barrier short instead (noted in the protocol).
  • Step 3 generators run on the catalog draft's placeholder densities (calibration: none); the owner's catalog entries (#1–#14) set the real distributions. Strain and g-factor draws wait for spin; switcher and drift rates tie to the catalog in Step 4. No screening in the charge potentials (upper bound) until Step 7.
  • ADR 0014: cross-platform tolerance raised from 1e-12 to 1e-9 after the layout-derived stability maps differed by 2e-11 between platforms (derived chains amplify last-bit differences at sharp steps). Typed chains still agree to 3e-14.
  • Step 2 still owes the P1 reproduction against a published layout (its reference entry does not exist yet; the owner names the paper) and the owner's sign-offs of its protocols. pinch-off-barrier from the layout is covered by turn-on-single-gate-layout (same sweep seen from the barrier side); say so if a separate picture is wanted.
  • Pages source is gh-pages (root); the docs root and per-PR previews are served.
  • Pages: ADR 0012 moves publishing to the gh-pages branch with per-PR previews at /pr-<n>/; the repository's Pages source must be set to that branch (root) once it exists, by the owner if the session is not permitted.
  • No protocol is signed off. The owner reviews the artifact, we iterate in chat, then a session writes docs/gallery/signoff/<id>.yaml at the owner's instruction (ADR 0008).
  • The two reference entries are proposed; no P1 test exists yet. The owner confirms or replaces them.
  • turn-on-single-gate and pinch-off-barrier are phenomenological shapes until Step 2.
  • Cross-platform bit identity failed on the first CI run of PR #19 (ten of eleven protocols; even pure exp/tanh curves differ in the last bit between the Ubuntu and Windows numpy builds). ADR 0010 now makes ubuntu-latest the reference platform for sign-off hashes and requires other platforms to agree within 1e-12 relative; the gallery-windows job compares to the reference artifact. Rule 3 in CLAUDE.md amended accordingly.
  • docs/catalog/entries/interface-fixed-charge.yaml still has free-text sources and no calibration field (warned, not failed, because it is draft).
  • Step 1 exit criteria still open: sign-offs; the benchmark is met locally (0.02 ms/point on stability-coarse-2dot, budget 0.1) but not yet confirmed on CI.

docs.title: 0001 — Two tiers: compile once per device instance, run cheap at every gate point
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-24 Step: all

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Faithful electrostatics (3D Poisson with screening) costs seconds to an hour per gate configuration; atomistic valley splitting costs hours; a tune-up sweeps ten thousand gate points. No model that solves physics at runtime can serve a tuning loop. Laplace is linear in the gate voltages, so a basis of potentials can be solved once; Hubbard parameters are smooth functions of barrier height; valley splitting is a draw.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Two tiers. compile runs the expensive physics once per device instance and emits a serialisable Device of parameter fields and functions; the runtime layers evaluate it at a gate point in under ~1 ms and never call a solver. Closed-form electrostatics (polygonal gates over a 2DEG) is the first compile path; FEM through a wrapped external solver is the second. Anything slower than the runtime budget moves to compile.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: ≥ 10⁴ gate points per second per core; scenarios are served pre-compiled; the runtime is pure numpy and portable.
  • Harder: two code paths for electrostatics; a compiled device must be versioned and serialised; nonlinear screening is approximated at runtime (parameter functions) rather than solved.
  • Must now: a benchmark in CI; model_version on every compiled device; the runtime budget in CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Solve physics at runtime with a fast solver — rejected: still ~10³× too slow for a loop.
  • Precompute full stability maps — rejected: the loop needs dynamics (rates, noise, latching), not images.

docs.title: 0002 — phantom claims statistical realism, never prediction of a particular device
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-24 Step: all

docs.title: Context
docs.text: What makes a device hard to tune is what is unknown about it: its disorder, defects and valley splittings. A model cannot know them, and the tuning loop exists to discover them. Overclaiming here would discredit the library with the people it serves.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A phantom instance behaves like a device of its class — the right kinds of faults at the right rates, the right sweep-rate dependence, the right readout behaviour — because its disorder is a draw from catalog distributions. phantom predicts classes, not devices. Documentation, APIs and any grading built on optimum state this; nothing in the library is named or described as predicting a specific device.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: the fidelity target is clear (P1 reproductions and P2 statistics), not a device-matching task.
  • Harder: consumers wanting a digital twin of one device must fit phantom's parameters to it themselves.
  • Must now: the P2 level compares distributions, not single devices; truth is labelled as the draw.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: • A digital twin fitted per device — out of scope; a consumer may build one on top.

docs.title: 0003 — phantom is a dependency-free library with a reproducibility contract; qdt consumes it through an adapter that lives in qdt
docs.text: Status: Accepted (rule 3 amended by 0010) Date: 2026-10-24 Step: 1, 8

docs.title: Context
docs.text: qdt's qdt-sim holds a double-dot model and noise models that implement qdt's instrument protocols. qdt decided (its ADR 0078) that the physics core stays a dependency-free module and is extracted once a second consumer exists; agent evaluation and hosted scenarios are those consumers, and both need ground truth and an optimum that must never travel through qdt's API.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• phantom imports nothing from qdt, measurement software or instrument SDKs; it is numpy/scipy in, numpy out. Its public API is plan §4: compile(...) -> Device, Device.at, Device.measure, Device.truth, optimum(Device), all versioned.
  • Reproducibility contract: parameters + seed + model_version → bit-identical output on every platform CI runs. A change that alters output bumps model_version.
  • qdt's adapter lives in qdt (qdt-sim): it maps StandConfig/ChannelMap onto a Device, implements qdt's capability protocols over it, pins a phantom release, and contains no physics (target: < 300 lines). phantom ships a contract test the adapter also runs.
  • Truth stays with the consumer. phantom exposes truth and optimum; a consumer that must hide them from a user (a tuning loop, a product, an agent) does not forward them. phantom never has a "hidden" mode.
  • Changes that break the adapter are breaking releases; qdt pins and upgrades deliberately (Step 8).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: three consumers share one physics with one version to cite; qdt's golden files depend on a pinned release, not a moving module.
  • Harder: physics changes reach qdt only through a release and a regeneration of its fixtures.
  • Must now: Step 8 cutover in qdt; a changelog; the contract test.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Keep physics in qdt-sim and have consumers import qdt — rejected: pulls qdt's schemas and protocols into every consumer; ground truth would sit behind qdt's API.
  • phantom exposes qdt's protocols directly — rejected: couples the library to one consumer's interface.

docs.title: 0004 — Nine layers that import only downward; compile imports all, nothing imports compile
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-24 Step: 0

docs.title: Context
docs.text: End-to-end realism needs layout, electrostatics, disorder, valley, charge, readout and spin, each with a different cost and a different source of truth. Without a dependency order the layers would entangle and the two-tier split (ADR 0001) would erode.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: layout ← electrostatics ← disorder ← valley ← charge ← readout ← spin ← optimum, each importing only layers below it; compile may import everything; nothing imports compile. scripts/check_imports.py enforces it, and the no-qdt rule, in CI. Each layer's __init__ docstring states what it owns and its runtime form.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: a consumer can use charge + readout without spin; layers are testable alone; the seam to extract or replace a layer (FEM electrostatics) is explicit.
  • Harder: cross-layer couplings (valley affecting readout, charge noise affecting spin) flow through parameters passed downward-to-upward, never by upward import.
  • Must now: keep the order in CLAUDE.md; a new layer is an ADR.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: • One flat model module — rejected: the entanglement this ADR exists to prevent.

docs.title: 0005 — Test ladder P0 (analytic limits), P1 (published results), P2 (device statistics, internal)
docs.text: Status: Superseded by 0007 (P2 removed; P0 and P1 stand) Date: 2026-10-24 Step: all

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A physics library needs its own notion of "proven," distinct from qdt's instrument ladder. The claims are statistical (ADR 0002), so the highest level compares distributions with real device statistics that are not public.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• P0 — analytic limits and invariants, in CI on every commit (Coulomb-diamond slopes, honeycomb geometry from a capacitance matrix, detailed balance, trace preservation, zero-severity draws reproduce the clean device bit for bit).
  • P1 — reproductions of published results, cited by DOI, in CI, marked literature, with the paper's stated tolerance.
  • P2 — comparisons with real device statistics (fault rates, sensor behaviour, tune-up time distributions), marked internal, run where that data lives, never committed here, and never an exit criterion for a step. A step exits when its P0 and P1 rows pass.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: the repo stays public and provenance-clean; fidelity has a citable basis.
  • Harder: some claims (fault rates) are only checkable at P2.
  • Must now: every P1 test names its source; -m 'not internal' is the default pytest selection.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: • Only P0 — rejected: invariants do not establish realism.

docs.title: 0006 — The defect and material catalog is data a human fills in; generators read it
docs.text: Status: Proposed Date: 2026-10-24 Step: 0, 3

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The map from fabrication defects and material traits to model perturbations is the knowledge an experienced tuner has and a model does not. Written as code it would be scattered across generators and hard to review; written as data it can be reviewed, cited, extended and argued about entry by entry.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: docs/catalog/ holds YAML entries (schema in docs/catalog/SCHEMA.md): id, name, material classes it applies to, the layer it perturbs, the parameter(s), the distribution and its defaults, a severity knob, the signature it leaves in a tune-up, a source, and a status (draft|reviewed|runtime|offline|rejected). disorder and compile read entries whose status is runtime or offline. Entries are filed as issues for a human to write (scripts/issues_catalog.py); a session may draft an entry but a human marks it reviewed. A catalog entry never contains a real device's values (CLAUDE.md rule 6).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: review per entry; the fault library grows without code changes once generators exist.
  • Harder: a schema to maintain; generators must handle unknown fields gracefully.
  • Must now: the template and schema in Step 0; the issue set filed.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: • Faults as code only — rejected: unreviewable by the person who knows them.

docs.title: 0007 — Validate against published results only; every claim names a reference entry
docs.text: Status: Accepted (supersedes 0005) Date: 2026-10-25 Step: all

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR 0005 defined three rungs: P0 analytic invariants, P1 published reproductions, P2 comparisons with internal device statistics. P2 was never an exit criterion and never entered the repo, but its existence let a quantity look "validated" by data nobody outside could see. For now the owner does not want the simulator matched against internal device data at all. The remaining standard is the literature, and the comparison with it must be explicit enough that a reader can open the paper.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Two rungs. P0 (analytic limits and invariants) and P1 (reproductions of published results) are the whole ladder. P2 is removed: the internal marker, the -m internal command and every mention of device statistics as a check go. A later ADR may bring it back; nothing here anticipates it.
  • A reference library, docs/references/, is the only admissible standard. One entry per paper (entries/<id>.yaml, schema in docs/references/SCHEMA.md): DOI, the layers it informs, and the concrete items it provides (a figure, a table, a value, a range) with the paper's own tolerance. Digitized curves live beside the entry under data/<id>/ with a note on how they were digitized.
  • Every claim cites an id. A P1 test is @pytest.mark.literature("<id>", item="<label>") and loads its reference curve from the library, never from a literal in the test. A catalog entry's sources and rate fields point to ids. Benchmarks and docs that claim agreement with physics name the id. scripts/check_references.py (in check_all.sh) fails on an id that does not exist, an entry whose id or DOI is malformed, or a literature test without an id.
  • Agent-proposed, human-confirmed. An entry is proposed when a session writes it and confirmed only after a human has opened the paper and checked the DOI, the figure and the digitized values. A P1 test against a proposed entry is skipped, not passed; a step cannot exit on it.
  • Uncalibrated is said out loud. A quantity with no published standard (some fault rates will be) is marked calibration: none in its catalog entry and its docstring. Nothing downstream may describe it as realistic. This is the cost of dropping P2 and it is stated rather than hidden.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: the repo's fidelity claim is auditable from public sources alone; provenance (rule 6) is trivially satisfied; a reader can reproduce every number.
  • Harder: fault rates and other device-population quantities are uncalibrated until a paper supplies them; a model can be fully "validated" and still be unconvincing, which ADR 0008 addresses.
  • Must now: check_references.py exists before the first P1 test; a session that writes an entry cannot flip it to confirmed; the catalog schema's sources field takes ids, not free text.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Keep P2 as documented in 0005 — rejected by the owner for now.
  • Free-text citations in tests — rejected: not checkable, and the digitized data would scatter.

docs.title: 0008 — A gallery of measurement protocols, rendered by CI, signed off per protocol by a human
docs.text: Status: Accepted (publishing amended by 0012: previews per pull request) Date: 2026-10-25 Step: all, from Step 1

docs.title: Context
docs.text: qdt has a front end, so a human could look at what the simulator produced. phantom has none and will not grow one (rule 7, ADR 0003). A passing P0 or P1 test says a number is right within tolerance; it does not let a human notice that a stability diagram looks wrong in a way nobody thought to assert. That judgement is the owner's, exercised in conversation with the agent, and it needs a durable record without an interactive UI in this repo.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Protocols, not tasks. The gallery is stratified by measurement protocol: a sweep definition in physics terms (gates, ranges, resolution, readout channel, time base, seed), one YAML file per protocol under docs/gallery/protocols/. Turn-on curves, barrier pinch-off, coarse and fine charge stability maps, Coulomb diamonds, sensor peaks, detuning cuts, noise time traces and spectra, later the spin-readout sweeps. These are the scans a tune-up uses, described as physics; a consumer maps them onto its own stages. Nothing here is named for a tuning step.
  • CI renders; git stores no images. scripts/gallery.py runs every protocol with its fixed seed and writes, outside git, the swept arrays (.npz), a PNG per protocol, the budget ledger (ADR 0009) and a mkdocs page. A gallery CI job uploads this as a workflow artifact on every PR and, on main, deploys the docs site with the gallery to GitHub Pages. Locally uv run python scripts/gallery.py then uv run mkdocs serve. matplotlib lives in the gallery dependency group, never in runtime deps.
  • Sign-off is on the data. A human signs a protocol by a record in docs/gallery/signoff/<id>.yaml: the canonical hash of the swept arrays, the generator commit, the model_versions involved, the seed, the date, the signer's GitHub handle, and the notes that came out of the review (what the sweep must show). CI recomputes the hash and fails if it differs from a signed record. Changing the physics therefore requires a new sign-off, which is the point.
  • Who writes the record. The human reviews the rendered gallery and discusses it with the agent in chat; the agent adjusts the protocol or the model and re-renders until the human says it is right. At the human's instruction the agent writes the sign-off record naming them; the human's approval of that PR is the signature. A session never signs on its own initiative.
  • Step exit. A step is settled only when every protocol its layers touch is rendered and signed off, in addition to P0 and P1 green (ADR 0007). The step files carry a fixed heading Gallery protocols.
  • Determinism. The arrays are covered by the reproducibility contract (rule 3) and must hash identically on both CI platforms. The PNG is for eyes only and is never compared.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: a human gate on realism without a UI in this repo; review happens where code review happens; the record of why a sweep looks the way it does survives the chat that produced it.
  • Harder: one more CI job and a Pages deployment; every physics change that moves a signed array needs a human in the loop before merge.
  • Must now: scripts/gallery.py, the protocol and sign-off schemas (docs/gallery/README.md), the CI job and the mkdocs nav exist in Step 1; each step lists its protocols before it starts.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Commit the PNGs — rejected by the owner: binaries in git; CI can render them on demand.
  • Pixel comparison of PNGs — rejected: matplotlib output is not platform-stable; the arrays are.
  • A notebook or interactive viewer in this repo — rejected: rule 7, and a maintenance burden phantom does not want.

docs.title: 0009 — Every gallery protocol carries a time and compute budget, measured in CI
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-25 Step: all, from Step 1

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A main application of phantom is the backend of a simulated measurement suite. A consumer sweeping a gate at interactive rates needs to know, per kind of measurement, how long a point costs and how much computation it buys. ADR 0001 sets the rule (compile once, run cheap, ~1 ms per gate point) but nothing tracks it per measurement, and regressions would be found by the consumer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Budget per protocol. Each protocol file (ADR 0008) declares a budget block with two phases, matching ADR 0001's tiers:
  • compile: wall seconds allowed for the once-per-instance setup, and the number of solver calls it may make.
  • run: wall milliseconds per point, the number of points, the number of model evaluations per point, and solver_calls: 0 always (runtime layers never call a solver, rule 4).
  • The gallery runner measures. scripts/gallery.py times both phases and counts evaluations and solver calls through a counter in the runner (not in the library), and writes budget.json with declared and measured values, per protocol, per platform.
  • Counts are strict, time is loose. Evaluation and solver counts are deterministic and CI compares them exactly. Wall time on shared runners is noisy, so CI fails only above a stated factor of the budget (3×, written in the runner), and prints the full table every run. Locally --strict applies the factor 1 for benchmarking.
  • Visible. The budget table is part of the rendered gallery page and the PR artifact, next to the pictures, so cost is reviewed with realism.
  • Changing a budget is a decision. Raising a protocol's budget goes in the PR description with the reason; lowering it is free.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: a consumer can read the cost of each measurement kind from one table; a change that makes a sweep slower is caught at the PR, with its cause attributed to a protocol.
  • Harder: every protocol author must think about cost up front; the runner carries counting hooks.
  • Must now: budget is a required block in the protocol schema; Step 1's benchmark deliverable (10⁴ gate points/s/core) is expressed as the budget of the two-dot stability protocol.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A single global benchmark — rejected: it hides which measurement regressed and says nothing to a consumer choosing a sweep.
  • Strict wall-time gates in CI — rejected: flaky on shared runners; counts carry the determinism.

docs.title: 0010 — Bit-for-bit reproducibility holds per platform; across platforms within 1e-12; ubuntu-latest is the reference
docs.text: Status: Accepted (amends 0003 rule 3 and 0008; tolerance amended by 0014) Date: 2026-10-25 Step: 1

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Rule 3 (ADR 0003) promised identical output, bit for bit, on every platform CI runs. The first cross-platform gallery run (PR #19) showed that ten of eleven protocols hash differently on ubuntu-latest and windows-latest, including two that evaluate nothing but exp, tanh and logaddexp of a gate voltage. numpy's elementary functions are dispatched to different SIMD and C-library implementations on the two builds and differ in the last unit of precision. No model written in numpy can promise bit identity across operating systems; the promise as written was false.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Per platform, bit for bit. For the same parameters, seed, model_version, operating system and numpy build, every output is identical byte for byte. This is what a consumer relies on: determinism by seed. CI asserts it by the Windows job and the Ubuntu job each reproducing their own fixtures.
  • Across platforms, within tolerance. Arrays produced on different platforms agree to a relative tolerance of 1e-12, measured per array as the largest absolute difference divided by the largest magnitude in the array. The tolerance is a constant in gallery/runner.py and is stated here.
  • One reference platform for sign-off. Sign-off records (ADR 0008) carry the array hash computed on ubuntu-latest in CI. That job is the reference. Every other platform's gallery job downloads the reference arrays and passes only if its own arrays agree within the tolerance; it reports a protocol as signed when the reference hash matches the record and its arrays agree with the reference.
  • Locally, on a machine that is not the reference platform, a hash mismatch against a sign-off is reported as "unverifiable here" rather than as a failure; the verdict belongs to CI.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: the contract is true and checkable; sign-off has one unambiguous hash.
  • Harder: a sign-off can only be verified exactly by the reference job; a change that moves an array by less than 1e-12 on another platform is invisible there, which is the intended meaning of the tolerance.
  • Must now: CLAUDE.md rule 3 reads as above; the gallery CI jobs are gallery (reference) and gallery-windows (compared to it); tests/test_qdt_sim_migration.py keeps its 1e-12 tolerances, which were already the honest ones.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Disable SIMD dispatch in numpy on CI — rejected: the C libraries' exp still differ, and consumers would not run with that setting.
  • Hash arrays rounded to a fixed number of digits — rejected: a value on a rounding boundary flips the hash at random; a tolerance comparison has no such edge.
  • Keep the claim and skip the check — rejected: an untestable promise is worse than a weaker one.

docs.title: 0011 — A running map of how the models fit together lives in the docs and is kept current
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-25 Step: 1 onward

docs.title: Context
docs.text: By the end of Step 1 the readout layer already has seven modules and the charge layer three, and a measurement is produced by chaining several of them (occupation, lead rates, latching, sensor, noise, demodulation). As later steps add electrostatics, disorder, valley and spin, a human reading the repo needs one place that says how these pieces combine to produce a measurement, and that place must not drift from the code.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• docs/MODELS.md holds two diagrams. The measurement flow is drawn by hand in Mermaid: boxes are models, arrows say which feeds which, placeholders that a later step replaces are dashed and name that step, and a table maps every gallery protocol to its path through the boxes. The module dependency graph is generated from the imports in src/phantom by scripts/model_graph.py.
  • A pull request that adds, removes or rewires a model updates the hand-drawn diagram and the protocol table in the same PR. check_all.sh runs scripts/model_graph.py --check, so the generated graph can never be stale; the hand-drawn one is reviewed like any other doc.
  • The page is in the mkdocs nav as "Models" and renders the Mermaid diagrams on the docs site.
  • Runtimes are recorded on the same page. scripts/gallery.py --record writes docs/gallery/measured.json: the measured cost of every protocol in that run and a per-model micro-benchmark (microseconds per point for each runtime model), with commit, platform and date. scripts/model_graph.py renders it into the page beside the declared budgets, and --check keeps the table in sync with the file. A session re-records when it changes a model or a protocol. The numbers are from the recording machine; the reference platform's numbers stay in the CI artifact (ADR 0010).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: a newcomer, or the owner reviewing a gallery picture, can trace which models produced it.
  • Harder: one more file to touch when a model changes; the hand-drawn diagram relies on review.
  • Must now: CLAUDE.md names the file in the End protocol and in "Where to look".

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Only the generated import graph — rejected: imports do not say what flows where, or what a placeholder is.
  • Only the hand-drawn diagram — rejected: it would drift; the generated graph anchors it to the code.

docs.title: 0012 — Every pull request publishes a preview of the docs and the rendered gallery; main publishes the root
docs.text: Status: Accepted (amends 0008) Date: 2026-10-25 Step: 1 onward

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR 0008 publishes the rendered gallery to GitHub Pages from main. The owner pointed out that this defeats the process it serves: review and sign-off are supposed to happen on the branch, before the merge, and a zip artifact or a hand-rebuilt page is a poor way to look at fourteen pictures and a budget table. The published site should carry the branch under review as well as the settled state.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A pages workflow builds the documentation site plus the rendered gallery for every push to a pull request and publishes it under /pr-<n>/ on the Pages site, served from the gh-pages branch. A sticky comment on the pull request carries the links (docs, rendered gallery, models and runtimes), updated on every push. When the pull request closes, its directory is removed.
  • Pushes to main publish the root of the site the same way. The root therefore always shows the settled state, and /pr-<n>/ shows what is being reviewed.
  • Pages is served from the gh-pages branch (deploy-from-branch), not from the Actions deployment, because only a branch can hold several directories at once.
  • Review and sign-off (ADR 0008) happen on the preview: the owner looks at /pr-<n>/gallery/rendered/, the discussion and the sign-off records land on the same branch, CI verifies the hashes, then the pull request merges.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: the gallery under review is one click from the pull request; nothing to download or rebuild.
  • Harder: the gh-pages branch accumulates deploy commits; previews of closed pull requests are removed by the workflow but the branch history keeps them.
  • Must now: the repository's Pages source is set to the gh-pages branch, root folder; the pages job leaves ci.yml; the gallery README points reviewers at the preview.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Keep publishing from main only and review the CI zip — rejected by the owner.
  • Separate hosting for previews — rejected: one site, one address scheme, nothing external.

docs.title: 0013 — Closed-form electrostatics: solid-angle potentials, effective depth, dots as harmonic minima
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-25 Step: 2

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Step 2 must turn a gate layout into the potential, the lever arms and the capacitance picture that the charge layer consumes, in microseconds at runtime (ADR 0001), without a field solver. Several modelling choices are needed to get there; each is an approximation a later step replaces, and each is the kind of thing a future session would ask "why?" about.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Potential. Davies–Larkin–Stern half-space electrostatics (reference entry davies1995-patterned-2deg): the potential under a gate at voltage V is V times the solid angle the gate polygon subtends at the point, over 2π. Implemented for any planar polygon as a fan of triangles (Van Oosterom–Strackee), not only rectangles; the rectangle arctangent form is kept as a test. Screening by the electrons is not included; Step 7's solver adds it.
  • Stack. The formula assumes one dielectric. A layered stack enters through an effective depth, Σ t_i · ε_well / ε_i: the thin-film approximation, exact for the normal field away from edges.
  • Dots. Dots are the deepest local minima of the electron potential energy inside the layout's channel region; the sensor dot likewise in its region. The dot radius is the harmonic ground-state length from the curvature at the minimum; its own capacitance is the disk value from that radius; its total capacitance divides by (1 − Σ_j α_j) so that the gate capacitances are part of it; the interdot mutual capacitance is the two-sphere estimate 4πε r₁ r₂ / s. Leads are not counted.
  • Lever arms are the basis values at the dot minimum (the dot as a point). The CI gate capacitances are then C_gate = C_dot · α, which makes the CI model's lever arms exactly the electrostatic ones; tested as the derivative of the dot energy with respect to each gate voltage.
  • Barriers are the maximum of the energy along the straight line between two minima, measured from the higher minimum.
  • Compile tier. Building the basis grid and finding dots is compile-tier (milliseconds); the runtime consumes the resulting ConstantInteractionParams. The finite-difference Schrödinger solve exists to check the harmonic estimate and for compile; runtime never calls it (rule 4).
  • Validation. P0 tests cover the closed form against its rectangle special case and known limits, the lever-arm derivative identity, the honeycomb period against the derived capacitance, and the Schrödinger spectrum against the harmonic oscillator. The P1 row of Step 2 compares lever arms and charging energies with a published layout once its reference entry is confirmed.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: a layout file alone yields potentials, lever arms and a stability diagram; numbers are in the right range for silicon dots (lever arms 0.05–0.25, charging energies of order 10 meV).
  • Harder: every quantity above the lever arms is an estimate with a stated approximation; fault models that depend on screening or on the exact dot shape wait for Step 7.
  • Must now: charge.derived is the only place the CI parameters are built from a layout; the approximations are repeated in its docstring; changes to them bump MODEL_VERSION.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A Poisson solver at runtime — rejected: ADR 0001.
  • Rectangles only — rejected: real layouts have rotated and L-shaped gates; the solid angle costs the same.
  • Typing the capacitances per layout — rejected: the point of Step 2 is that they are derived.

docs.title: 0014 — The cross-platform tolerance is 1e-9 relative, because derived parameter chains amplify last-bit differences
docs.text: Status: Accepted (amends 0010) Date: 2026-10-26 Step: 2

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR 0010 set the cross-platform agreement of gallery arrays at 1e-12 relative, measured per array as the largest difference over the largest magnitude. Every Step 1 protocol met it with margin (worst 3e-14). The first Step 2 protocols that derive their parameters from a layout did not: stability-coarse-2dot-layout and crosstalk-lines differ between ubuntu-latest and windows-latest by 1.5e-11 and 2.0e-11. The chain solid angle (arctangents) → lever arms → capacitance matrix inverse → gate-voltage of the sensor flank → Boltzmann occupation turns a last-bit difference in an elementary function into a shift of a transition position of order 1e-14 V, and at a pixel that sits on a sharp step that shift is a relative change of order 1e-11 in the current. Nothing is wrong with either platform's result; the tolerance was tighter than the arithmetic allows for derived chains with sharp features.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The cross-platform tolerance (CROSS_PLATFORM_RTOL in gallery/runner.py) is 1e-9 relative, per array, with the same definition as ADR 0010. A genuine change to physics or parameters moves arrays by 1e-6 or more, so the check still catches every real change; what it stops flagging is arithmetic noise amplified through derived chains.
  • Everything else in ADR 0010 stands: bit-for-bit per platform, ubuntu-latest the reference for sign-off hashes, the Windows job compared to the reference.
  • Rounding derived parameters to suppress the noise was considered and rejected again for the reason in ADR 0010: a value on a rounding boundary flips.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: layout-derived protocols pass on both platforms without special cases.
  • Harder: a change that moves an array by less than 1e-9 relative is invisible to the Windows check; the reference platform's exact hash (sign-off) still sees it.
  • Must now: CLAUDE.md rule 3 and the gallery README say 1e-9; the measured worst cases are recorded here (3e-14 for typed chains, 2e-11 for derived chains, both on 2026-10-26).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Per-protocol tolerances — rejected: one number is easier to reason about and 1e-9 is loose enough.
  • Comparing occupations instead of currents — rejected: the sensor current is what the protocol measures.

docs.title: 0015 — Disorder generators: interface charges as image-charge energy offsets, lithography faults as polygon transforms, one seeded scenario draw
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-26 Step: 3

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Step 3 turns catalog entries into generators that perturb the device for physical reasons. The catalog entries themselves (#1–#14) are the owner's to write, and only the draft interface-fixed-charge exists, with placeholder densities. The generators must be buildable now, on parameters, and must fit the closed-form electrostatics of Step 2 (ADR 0013) without a solver.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Interface charges (disorder.charges): a Poisson number of point charges ±e at the interface depth over the layout's bounding box, density × severity. Each adds to the electron energy in the electron plane the potential of the charge plus its image in the pinned surface (the same half-space model as the gate potentials), with a smoothing length for the finite thickness of the electron layer so that charges in the plane itself (MOS) stay finite. No screening by the electrons; the perturbation is an upper bound and the entry is calibration: none until a confirmed reference sets density and sign.
  • Gate misalignment and width error (disorder.geometry_faults): a common shift of the gate layer and an independent outward edge displacement per gate, applied to the polygons. The perturbed lever-arm basis follows from the electrostatics with no new physics.
  • The landscape carries disorder as an offset: GateBasis.offset_ev is a gate-independent energy added to the electron energy; everything above (dot finding, derived CI parameters, sensor coupling) works unchanged on a perturbed basis.
  • One scenario draw (disorder.scenario): material-class parameters + seed + severity → all generators from one generator stream, in a fixed order; to_dict()/from_dict() make the draw plain data a consumer can store. Severity 0 draws nothing and returns the clean layout and basis, bit for bit (P0 test).
  • Constants live in phantom.constants, below every layer, so disorder imports nothing from charge (rule 2).
  • Protocols: the landscape and the coarse stability map, clean beside three draws; and the mean number of unintentional minima against charge density over many draws, which the Step 3 P1 row will compare with a published MOS/SiGe comparison.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: disorder is a few hundred microseconds of compile-tier work per draw; every Step 1 and Step 2 protocol can be rendered for a draw by passing a perturbed basis.
  • Harder: without screening, charge densities at the MOS placeholder give large perturbations; the numbers are placeholders until the catalog is written, and nothing here claims a rate.
  • Must now: strain and g-factor draws wait for the spin layer; switchers and drift remain noise processes in readout (Step 4 ties their rates to the catalog); the catalog entry gains calibration: none and tier: runtime.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Random potential fields with a chosen correlation length — rejected: not traceable to a catalog quantity.
  • Screened (Thomas–Fermi) charge potentials — deferred to Step 7's solver tier (ADR 0001).

docs.title: 0016 — Wiring faults as a gate matrix and a leak network; sensor asymmetry as coupling draws; trapping as a history state
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-10-26 Step: 3

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Three catalog entries describe faults with trivial physics but common occurrence: an open or shorted gate (#4), gate-to-gate leakage (#3) and sensor–dot coupling asymmetry (#11). A fourth signature, the hysteresis loop of a gate sweep, comes from charge trapping with gate history (#1 at its slowest). Step 3 needs generators for all four that fit the existing chain without new electrostatics.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Wiring faults (disorder.wiring) act on the gate vector before the basis: the voltages the gates actually carry are M·V + c for programmed V. A shorted pair copies the kept gate's row onto the follower; an open gate zeroes its row and sets a stuck potential. Protocols sweep programmed voltages, so the signature appears where a tune-up would see it.
  • Leakage is a resistance network between adjacent gate pairs; the current out of each gate is the sum over its leaks, equal and opposite on the two ends. It adds to the dielectric leakage of readout.transport in the leakage protocols.
  • Sensor asymmetry scales each dot's per-electron sensor coupling by a log-normal factor.
  • Adjacent pairs are defined geometrically from the layout (polygons within 30 nm in the same band), so the fault model follows the design.
  • Trapping (disorder.trapping) is a trapped fraction with first-order kinetics per sample along the gate sequence: charging above a capture voltage, releasing below a release voltage, holding between. The effective gate voltage is V − shift × f. It is static and history-dependent, the slow partner of the telegraph and 1/f processes in readout.noise; Step 4 ties the rates of both to the catalog.
  • All four are part of the scenario draw (wiring), seeded, serialisable, and clean at severity 0; probabilities and parameters are placeholders (calibration: none) until the entries are written.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Easier: the fault signatures (faint dot, gates moving together, floating barrier, leak current pair, hysteresis loop) render from the same layout and models as the clean device.
  • Harder: a shorted or open gate can leave the intended dots unformed at the clean operating point; protocols that derive dots must handle the failure (they re-derive at the actual voltages).
  • Must now: readout.transport turn-on protocols accept a trapping draw; Step 4 connects the trap kinetics to the fluctuator rates.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Faults as perturbations of the derived CI parameters — rejected: the signature of a short is in how programmed voltages map to the device, which the gate matrix captures and a CI tweak would not.
  • A full trap ensemble with capture and emission time constants — deferred to Step 4.

docs.title: Defect and material catalog
docs.text:
The knowledge only an experienced tuner has: which defects and material traits exist, what they perturb, and what they look like during tune-up. Data, not code (ADR 0006). Schema: SCHEMA.md. Entries: entries/*.yaml. One example entry is provided as a draft with every value marked TODO; the rest are filed as GitHub issues by scripts/issues_catalog.py for a human to write.

Suggested entries (the issue set): interface fixed charge · oxide traps and two-level fluctuators · gate misalignment and width error · gate-to-gate overlap and leakage · open or shorted gate · Ge-concentration fluctuation (valley) · interface steps and roughness · strain variation · residual dopants · dielectric thickness variation · 2DEG density and mobility by material class · sensor-dot coupling asymmetry · charge drift (slow) · material classes SiGe vs MOS as summary traits · (later) Ge holes.

docs.text:
One YAML file per entry under docs/catalog/entries/, named <id>.yaml. Fields:

Rules: no real device, wafer or site values; published values cite their paper; a session may write a draft, only a human sets reviewed.

docs.title: Gallery (ADR 0008, 0009)
docs.text:
A stratified set of measurement protocols: sweeps a device of this class is put through, described as physics (gates, ranges, resolution, readout channel, time base, seed). CI renders every protocol on every PR; nothing rendered is stored in git. A human signs each protocol off; a step is settled only when all protocols its layers touch are signed.

View it. On a pull request: the preview link in the sticky comment on the PR, which points at https://cowboyquantum.github.io/phantom/pr-<n>/gallery/rendered/index.html (ADR 0012); it updates a minute or two after each push and is removed when the PR closes. On main: the docs site, "Gallery" in the nav, then the rendered gallery. The CI artifact gallery-ubuntu-latest holds the same files. Locally:

uv run python scripts/gallery.py          # renders to build/gallery/ (gitignored)
uv run mkdocs serve                       # browse it

The candidate roster for every step is PROTOCOLS.md; rows become protocol files when their step opens.

The only admissible standard for a claim that phantom agrees with physics. One entry per paper under entries/<id>.yaml (schema: SCHEMA.md); digitized curves under data/<id>/.

docs.title: Step 1 — Charge and readout core
docs.text: Fixed headings. Agents read this file for the current step; the narrative is in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Migrate qdt-sim's DoubleDotModel and noise models into charge and readout as the seed, strip every qdt dependency, make parameters explicit functions of gate voltage, prove the reproducibility contract, and stand up the validation tooling every later step uses: the reference library check, the gallery renderer with budgets, and the CI job that publishes it.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• charge: Dot, Barrier, a two-dot constant-interaction model and a Hubbard model with t(V_barrier) exponential, U(dot size), V_ij; ground-state charge per gate point
  • readout: SensorSET conductance vs. gate with capacitive coupling to dots; noise processes (white, telegraph, 1/f, fluctuator ensemble) with explicit time stepping; a sensor_lockin channel: the demodulated sensor response to a square-wave modulation of a named gate (amplitude, frequency), so a hardware derivative map is a protocol, not a post-processing step
  • Reproducibility: seed + model_version → bit-identical arrays; a cross-platform CI job
  • scripts/check_references.py in check_all.sh; the first reference entries (proposed) for the quantities the P0/P1 rows below depend on (ADR 0007)
  • scripts/gallery.py: runs every protocol, writes arrays, PNGs, budget.json and a mkdocs page to build/gallery/; verifies sign-off hashes; gallery dependency group with matplotlib (ADR 0008, 0009)
  • CI: gallery job uploading the artifact on every PR; Pages deployment of the docs site from main
  • Benchmark: ≥ 10⁴ gate points/s/core on a 2-dot Hubbard model, expressed as the run budget of stability-coarse-2dot

docs.title: P0 tests (CI: analytic limits and invariants)
docs.text:
• single-dot Coulomb diamonds: slopes equal the lever arms; addition energy equals U
  • two-dot honeycomb: triple-point spacing from the CI capacitance matrix
  • Hubbard limit t → 0 reproduces the CI model
  • noise: PSD of the 1/f process matches its parameter within tolerance; telegraph rates match
  • gallery arrays hash identically on both platforms; declared counts match measured counts

docs.title: P1 tests (CI, literature: reproduce an item of a confirmed reference entry; ADR 0007)
docs.text: • none yet; candidates: honeycomb geometry and lever arms from a review of few-electron double dots; a 1/f charge-noise amplitude at 1 Hz for Si MOS or SiGe. Entries are proposed in this step and confirmed by a human before a test is written.

docs.title: Gallery protocols (rendered by CI, signed off per protocol by a human; ADR 0008)
docs.text:
• turn-on-single-gate: current vs. one plunger, others fixed; shows a threshold and saturation
  • pinch-off-barrier: current vs. one barrier gate; shows exponential pinch-off
  • coulomb-oscillations-single-dot: current vs. plunger with barriers set; periodic peaks spaced by the addition energy
  • diamonds-single-dot: current vs. (plunger, bias); Coulomb diamonds with slopes from the lever arms
  • stability-coarse-2dot: charge state or sensor signal vs. (P1, P2), wide range; honeycomb
  • stability-fine-2dot: same, zoomed on one triple-point pair; interdot line with tunnel-coupling broadening
  • stability-lockin-p1, -p2, -common, -detuning: the coarse region read through sensor_lockin with the chop on P1, on P2, on both (common mode) and in opposition (detuning); with lead-rate dynamics (readout.loading.LeadRateLandscape): latching where the rate is below the chop frequency, lifetime broadening where it is far above
  • docs/MODELS.md measurement-flow diagram and generated module graph (ADR 0011)
  • plunger-vs-barrier-map: sensor signal vs. (P1, lead barrier of dot 1), dot 1 the only dot with a reservoir; line tilt from the lever arm and latching as the barrier closes (minimal loading model in readout.loading, replaced in Step 4)
  • sensor-coulomb-peak: sensor conductance vs. sensor plunger; a peak and its slope
  • noise-time-trace: sensor signal vs. time at a fixed point; telegraph and drift visible
  • noise-psd: power spectral density of the trace; the 1/f slope and white floor Full roster with later steps: docs/gallery/PROTOCOLS.md. Each carries a budget; each is unsigned until the owner has reviewed it in the PR artifact.

docs.title: Step 2 — Layout and closed-form electrostatics
docs.text: Fixed headings. Agents read this file for the current step; the narrative is in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A gate layout and a material stack give V(r; gate vector) in microseconds; dots and barriers emerge from the potential; lever-arm fields and the capacitance matrix are derived, not typed.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• layout: gate polygons, stack (2DEG depth, dielectric layers), material class (SiGe, MOS) with their default parameters; JSON in and out; the textbook two_dot_layout() (done)
  • electrostatics: Davies–Larkin–Stern closed-form potential for polygonal gates over a 2DEG as the solid angle of any polygon; per-gate basis; superposition; dots as minima with harmonic radii, barriers as saddles; a 2D effective-mass Schrödinger solve, offline (done; ADR 0013)
  • charge reads lever arms and barrier heights from electrostatics instead of constants: charge.derived.derive_double_dot builds the CI parameters from a layout (done)
  • reference entries (proposed) for the closed-form potential and for the published layout the P1 row reproduces (ADR 0007)

docs.title: P0 tests (CI: analytic limits and invariants)
docs.text:
• a single rectangular gate's potential matches the closed form at known points
  • lever arms from the basis equal the capacitance-matrix values for a textbook two-dot layout
  • a two-dot layout yields a honeycomb whose geometry matches Step 1's CI model within tolerance

docs.title: P1 tests (CI, literature: reproduce an item of a confirmed reference entry; ADR 0007)
docs.text: • lever arms and charging energies for a published single-layer SiGe layout within the paper's stated range

docs.title: Gallery protocols (rendered by CI, signed off per protocol by a human; ADR 0008)
docs.text:
• potential-map-layout: V(x, y) in the 2DEG plane at a named gate setting, gate polygons overlaid; two wells and the barriers between them visible (rendering)
  • potential-cut-along-channel: V along the dot-to-dot axis for several barrier voltages; the barrier height falls as the gate opens (rendering)
  • stability-coarse-2dot-layout: the coarse map with nothing typed but the layout, the operating point and the sensor's per-electron coupling; the sensor gate is set on its flank first (rendering)
  • gate-leakage-iv: leakage current vs. each gate; ~0 in the safe window, onset at the extremes (rendering; proportional to gate area, phenomenological)
  • ohmic-iv: current vs. source–drain bias with all gates accumulated; linear (rendering; phenomenological)
  • turn-on-global: current vs. all gates swept together; threshold from the layout's channel barrier (rendering)
  • pinch-off-crosstalk: pinch-off voltage of one barrier vs. another gate's voltage; a straight line whose slope is the cross-capacitance ratio (rendering; step shape phenomenological)
  • crosstalk-lines: sensor signal vs. four gate pairs; the lever-arm matrix from the line slopes (rendering)
  • gate-hysteresis: one gate up then down; the two traces overlap for a clean device (rendering; the loop appears in Step 3)
  • turn-on-single-gate-layout: the Step 1 turn-on re-rendered from the layout's channel barrier (rendering)
  • still to do: the P1 reproduction against a published layout (owner names the paper); sign-offs Full roster: docs/gallery/PROTOCOLS.md. Each carries a budget; each is unsigned until the owner has reviewed it in the PR artifact.

docs.title: Step 3 — Disorder and the fault models
docs.text: Fixed headings. Agents read this file for the current step; the narrative is in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Catalog entries become generators that perturb the compiled potential and parameters, so unintentional dots, leaky barriers, asymmetric lever arms, charge switchers and drift appear for physical reasons and at catalog-set rates.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• disorder: static random interface/oxide charges (density per material class) added to the potential basis as image-charge energy offsets (done, ADR 0015); gate misalignment and width error as polygon transforms (done); strain and g-factor perturbations as parameter draws (waits for spin)
  • fault generators for every catalog entry marked runtime, each with a severity knob: interface charges, misalignment and width error, open and shorted gates, gate-to-gate leakage, sensor-coupling asymmetry, trapping hysteresis (done on placeholders, ADR 0015/0016); valley, strain, dopants, drift wait for their layers or Step 4
  • a scenario draw: material + catalog + seed → a perturbed device, serialisable (disorder.scenario, done; parameters are the catalog draft's placeholders until the entries are written)

docs.text:

  • a draw with zero severity reproduces the clean device bit for bit

docs.title: Gallery protocols (rendered by CI, signed off per protocol by a human; ADR 0008)
docs.text:
• potential-map-disorder: the landscape of the clean layout beside three draws, gate outlines overlaid (rendering)
  • stability-coarse-2dot-disorder: the layout-derived coarse map, clean beside three draws each re-derived from its own landscape (rendering)
  • unintentional-dots: mean extra minima in the channel against charge density over many draws, MOS class (rendering; the P1 row's curve)
  • fault-signatures-stability: the coarse map with clean wiring and three named faults: a weakly coupled dot, a shorted plunger–barrier pair, an open barrier (rendering)
  • gate-leakage-pair: a gigaohm leak between two neighbouring gates against the healthy curve (rendering)
  • gate-hysteresis-trapping: the turn-on swept up and down with trapping, the loop against the clean baseline (rendering)
  • to come: switcher and drift rates tied to the catalog (Step 4); fault signatures in the lock-in and plunger-barrier maps as the owner asks

  • the fault signatures listed in the catalog are visible in rendered diagrams reviewed by the human
